newsitem.title: USA: Attorneys general discuss dividing up tobacco pot.
newsitem.headline: Attorneys general discuss dividing up tobacco pot.

text.p: State attorneys general who hammered out a landmark $368.5 billion settlement with the tobacco industry were turning on Monday to the thorny question of how the money should be divided up.

Although it did not appear anywhere in the agenda, the tobacco agreement was set to be a key issue at this week's meeting of the National Association of Attorneys General at a lodge in the majestic surroundings of the Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming.
Attorneys general who led the long and arduous negotiations with the tobacco industry were expected to brief their colleagues at this week's conference.
A private meeting to discuss the agreement was set for Monday afternoon, conference participants said.
Cigarette companies agreed last Friday to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate states for treating smoking-related illnesses and to fund national anti-smoking programs.
The agreement will be closely scrutinized by the Clinton administration and by Congress. Some critics have already complained that the agreement is not tough enough.

Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey, who has labeled the agreement "woefully inadequate", was expected to voice his objections at this week's meeting of the top state law enforcement officials.
The attorneys general will also discuss how to divide up the tobacco money between the states, which differ greatly in population and how much they have spent on treating smoking- related illness.
Another possible point of contention is that, while 40 states sued the tobacco industry, some joined the suit far later than others.

"There's a lot of details left unresolved that really have to be resolved amongst ourselves ... with respect to, for example, dividing the pie, what type of formula you use," said Maine Attorney General Andrew Ketterer.

Maine was the state with the highest percentage of people aged 18 to 30 who smoke. "To me that would be a good way of dividing the pie. I'm sure California would say: 'Well, why don't we do it based on Medicaid dollars'," he told Reuters.

He said the issue of dividing the pie had the potential to be contentious. "I think what people have to keep in mind is how far we've come. We were at ground zero. To get from there to here I think is pretty amazing," Ketterer, a Democrat, said.

"Starting (Monday), we need to begin to discuss the internal allocation formula, on how states will allocate the moneys. That's an important discussion. I'm optimistic ...," New Jersey Attorney General Peter Verniero, a Republican, said.
"Fairness will be the guiding principle I hope. It has been up to this point," he said.
"We had several objectives in filing suit and I believe all of our objectives have been satisfied and I hope Congress will act expeditiously to accept the settlement," he added.
Ohio Attorney General Betty Montgomery, a Republican, said she believed every state should get a share of the proceeds regardless of whether or not they joined the suit.

She said the attorneys general had "a pretty clear understanding that this has to be divided ... among litigating and non-litigating states equally," although she believed that states that filed suit early on should be reimbursed for their costs.
